bridge: From M03, count outcomes; from M01, interpret a fraction and percentage. For example, 3 of 10 is 3/10=0.3=30%. A percentage means “out of a hundred”. Readiness check: 20 of 1000 is 2%, not 20%.
teaching:
Start with a collection you can count. If 3 of 10 equally likely cards are marked, the chance of selecting a marked card is 3/10. A probability is between 0 and 1: zero means impossible under the model and one means certain. The collection and the selection rule matter. Unequally likely cards need unequal weights rather than simply “favourable cards divided by all cards”.

Conditioning means keeping only cases where something is already known. P(A|B), read “probability of A given B”, asks what fraction of the B cases also have A. If we ask “of all alerts, which are real incidents?”, first gather the alerts, not the whole population. Reversing the question gives a different group: “of all real incidents, which caused an alert?”

Give the four cells names: a true positive (TP) is a real incident that alerted; a false positive (FP) is a benign event that alerted; a false negative (FN) is a missed incident; a true negative (TN) is a benign event that did not alert. Precision is TP divided by all alerts, TP+FP. Recall, also called sensitivity here, is TP divided by all incidents, TP+FN. Build these counts before reaching for a formula.

Probability assigns weights to an outcome space. Conditional probability P(A|B) asks about A after restricting attention to cases where B occurs. Independence means learning B does not change A's probability; it is an assumption to justify, not a synonym for events having different names.

A base rate is the frequency of the condition before considering a test. Even a sensitive detector can produce mostly false alarms when true incidents are rare. Use counts to avoid confusing P(alert|incident) with P(incident|alert). Precision asks what fraction of alerts are real; recall asks what fraction of real incidents alerted.

Entropy measures uncertainty under a distribution. For a fair bit it is one bit. Two equally likely independent bits have four equally likely outcomes and two bits of entropy. Four possible labels do not imply two bits if one label dominates. Predictable random-number seeds can make generated values unsuitable for security even when their printed distribution looks varied.

Conditional probability asks about A after restricting attention to cases where B happened. The formal rule is \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\), for \(P(B)>0\). Bayes’ rule writes the same intersection in two ways: \(P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)\). Include every way the observed event can occur in the denominator; the alert table below shows why.

Independence means \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). This form also handles zero-probability events without conditioning on them. Pairwise independence checks each pair. Mutual independence requires the product rule for every subcollection. A large sample alone establishes neither condition.

A discrete random variable assigns a number to each outcome. Its expectation is \(E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x)\). This weighted average need not itself be a possible observed outcome. Where the expectations exist, \(E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]\) even when \(X,Y\) are dependent.

For a finite distribution, entropy is \(H(X)=-\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)\). It describes uncertainty in that distribution. A zero-probability term contributes zero, using its limiting value.

A collision means two independent draws produce the same value. With N equally likely values, k draws create k(k−1)/2 pairs that could collide. Before collisions become common, the collision probability is approximately \(k(k-1)/(2N)\). The birthday scale is \(\sqrt{N}\): for a 16-bit space, \(N=2^{16}=65536\) and \(\sqrt{N}=256\). At 256 draws the exact probability is about 39%, so this is a warning scale, not a guarantee or an exact 50% threshold. For n-bit uniformly random values, the scale is \(2^{n/2}\), much smaller than exhausting all \(2^n\) values. Nonuniform or correlated draws can be worse. This matters when estimating whether randomly chosen nonces may repeat; a construction may require a stricter uniqueness rule.
example:
Population: 10,000 events
Real incidents: 100; benign: 9,900
Detector catches 90 incidents and alerts on 99 benign events.
                  alert  no alert
incident            90       10
benign              99     9801
Precision = 90/(90+99) ≈ 47.6%
Recall    = 90/(90+10) = 90%
explanation: Read one row at a time. There are 100 real incidents: 90 alerted and 10 did not. There are 9,900 benign events: 99 alerted and 9,801 did not. The row totals add to 10,000, so no event is missing. The alert column has \(90+99=189\) events. Of those, 90 are true incidents, giving precision \(90/189\approx0.476=47.6\%\). For recall, keep the incident row: \(90/(90+10)=90\%\). The detector finds many incidents, yet more than half its alerts concern benign events. That happens because benign events are much more common. Choosing whether this burden is acceptable requires the costs of review and missed incidents, not a single “accuracy” slogan.
exercise: Use a second population: 1,000 events, 20 incidents, 15 detected incidents and 35 false alerts. Fill all four matrix cells, calculate precision and recall, and state the number of missed incidents. For a uniformly random 24-bit value, estimate the birthday collision scale. Explain why it is smaller than the number of available values.
solution: Start with the incident row: 20 incidents minus 15 detected gives 5 misses, so TP=15 and FN=5. There are \(1000-20=980\) benign events; subtract the 35 false alerts to get TN=945. All four cells sum to 1000. All alerts total \(15+35=50\), so precision is \(15/50=30\%\). All incidents total 20, so recall is \(15/20=75\%\). If your denominators are reversed, restate the question in words before recalculating. For 24 bits, \(\sqrt{2^{24}}=2^{12}=4096\) draws is the birthday scale. Many pairs are being compared, so a repeat can become plausible long before all \(2^{24}\) values are used.
challenge: A detector is applied to 100 events, including 10 incidents. It catches 8 incidents and alerts on 18 benign events. Calculate precision, recall and total alerts. Explain why independent trials would be an unsafe assumption for repeated events from one device.
challenge_solution: Precision=8/26≈30.8%; recall=80%; alerts=26. Events from one device may share configuration or a single incident and be correlated. Treating them as independent can overstate the amount of evidence.
